ai_generated_text: Integrated Circuit Layout Integrated circuit layout, also known as IC layout or mask layout, is the representation of an integrated circuit (IC) in terms of planar geometric shapes that correspond to the patterns of metal, oxide, or semiconductor layers of the manufacturing process. It serves as the blueprint for fabricating the physical structure of a microchip and is a critical step in the design flow of semiconductor devices. The layout defines the spatial arrangement of transistors, interconnects, contacts, and other components on a silicon wafer, translating circuit schematics into physical structures that can be manufactured using photolithography. ##Purpose and Importance The primary purpose of IC layout is to convert an abstract circuit design into a manufacturable format that adheres to the design rules of a specific semiconductor fabrication process. The layout ensures that the electrical characteristics of the circuit - such as signal integrity, power consumption, and performance - are preserved during fabrication. Errors in layout can lead to functional failures, reduced yield, or reliability issues in the final product. Therefore, layout accuracy and optimization are essential for achieving high performance, low power, and cost-effective chip production. ##Design Rules and Constraints IC layout must comply with a set of design rules established by the semiconductor foundry. These rules specify minimum feature sizes, spacing between features, and overlay tolerances to ensure that the circuit can be reliably manufactured using photolithographic and etching processes. Design rules vary depending on the technology node (e.g., 7 nm, 5 nm) and the specific fabrication process (e.g., CMOS, FinFET). Violations of these rules - known as design rule violations (DRVs) - are detected using design rule checking (DRC) software tools. In addition to physical constraints, layout must account for electrical considerations such as parasitic capacitance, resistance, and inductance. These parasitic effects can significantly impact circuit behavior, especially at high frequencies or in analog and mixed-signal designs. Techniques such as matched device placement, shielding, and careful routing are employed to minimize such effects. ##Layout Design Process The IC layout process typically follows these stages: 1. Schematic Capture: The circuit is first designed at the schematic level, specifying components and their interconnections. 2. Floorplanning: High-level placement of major functional blocks (e.g., CPU cores, memory arrays) is determined to optimize area, power, and signal routing. 3. Placement: Individual transistors, standard cells, or macro blocks are positioned on the chip according to timing, power, and routing constraints. 4. Routing: Conductive paths (wires) are created to connect components, using multiple metal layers stacked vertically and separated by dielectric materials. Routing must avoid shorts, ensure signal integrity, and minimize delays. 5. Verification: The layout undergoes several checks: Design Rule Checking (DRC): Ensures compliance with fabrication constraints. Layout Versus Schematic (LVS): Confirms that the physical layout matches the original circuit schematic. Parasitic Extraction (PEX): Extracts parasitic elements for accurate simulation. Electrical Rule Checking (ERC): Validates electrical integrity. 6. Tape-out: Once verified, the final layout is converted into a format suitable for photomask generation (e.g., GDSII or OASIS) and sent to the fabrication facility. ##Tools and Automation Modern IC layout is performed using electronic design automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso, Synopsys Custom Compiler, and Siemens Tanner. These tools provide graphical interfaces for manual layout as well as automated functions for placement, routing, and verification. Full-custom layout is often used for analog, RF, and high-performance digital circuits, where precise control over device geometry and placement is required. In contrast, semi-custom or standard-cell design methodologies rely on pre-characterized cells and automated place-and-route tools for digital logic, enabling faster design cycles. ##Challenges in Advanced Nodes As semiconductor technology advances to smaller process nodes, IC layout faces increasing challenges: Process Variability: At nanometer scales, minor variations in lithography and etching can significantly affect device performance. Interconnect Delay: Wire resistance and capacitance become dominant factors, requiring careful routing and use of low-k dielectrics. Power Integrity: Managing IR drop and electromigration in power distribution networks is critical. Thermal Management: High-density layouts generate more heat, necessitating thermal-aware design. Multiple Patterning: Advanced lithography techniques like EUV and multi-patterning impose additional layout constraints. ##Conclusion Integrated circuit layout is a foundational discipline in semiconductor design, bridging the gap between circuit theory and physical realization. It requires a deep understanding of both electrical engineering and semiconductor physics, as well as proficiency in specialized EDA tools.

original_text: The Newport Rising was the last large-scale armed protest in Great Britain, seeking democracy and the right to vote with a secret ballot. On Monday 4 November 1839, approximately 4,000 Chartist sympathisers, under the leadership of John Frost, marched on the town of Newport, Monmouthshire. En route, some Newport chartists were arrested by police and held prisoner at the Westgate Hotel in central Newport. Marchers from industrial towns outside of Newport, including many coal-miners, some with home-made arms, were intent on liberating their fellow Chartists. On their demands that the protesters were freed, soldiers of the 45th Regiment of Foot, deployed in the protection of the police, were ordered to open fire at the crowd, turning the protest effectively into a pitched hand-to-hand battle. About 22 demonstrators were confirmed killed, whilst reports of perhaps a further 50 injured. 4 soldiers were reported as injured. Subsequently, the leaders of the march were convicted of treason and were sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered. The sentence was later commuted to transportation. Causes The origins
